bank.text: The Arkansas Alligator Farm opened on Whittington Avenue in 1902.
H. L. Campbell founded the farm in 1902, wanting a tourist draw beyond the baths.
bank.source: Wikipedia: Arkansas Alligator Farm and Petting Zoo

bank.text: Campbell brought the first alligators from the Florida Everglades.
bank.source: Encyclopedia of Arkansas: Arkansas Alligator Farm and Petting Zoo

bank.text: Around 1929, under owner Danny Older, it was called the Hot Springs Gator Farm.
bank.source: Encyclopedia of Arkansas: Arkansas Alligator Farm and Petting Zoo

bank.text: The early museum showed a "Merman," said to be a mummified sea creature. (A sideshow legend!)
bank.source: Encyclopedia of Arkansas: Arkansas Alligator Farm and Petting Zoo

bank.text: On March 17, 1918, Babe Ruth hit a home run that landed in the Alligator Farm.
Ruth hit that 1918 homer at Whittington Park, right across the street from the farm.
bank.source: KNWA/KFTA: The home run that made Babe Ruth a star

research.text: An alligator has 74 to 80 teeth at a time and can go through about 3,000 in a lifetime.
Nest temperature decides whether alligator eggs hatch as males or females.
A mother alligator usually lays 35 to 50 eggs, which hatch after about 65 days.
Adult male alligators average about 11.2 feet long; females about 8.2 feet.
Alligators dig "gator holes" and mud tunnels up to 65 feet long to ride out hot and cold weather.
Arkansas protected its alligators in 1961, when they were left only in the state's southwest corner.
From 1972 to 1984, Arkansas released 2,841 alligators brought from Louisiana.
The farm is home to about 200 adult and baby alligators.
Every 10 to 15 years the farm gets a permit for 12 to 15 baby alligators from Louisiana.
Summer feeding shows at noon serve up about 200 pounds of chicken.
Small gators held for photos sometimes have their mouths held shut with rubber bands.
Hot Springs winters are cold, so the gators spend about six months a year in a barn under heat lamps.
About 50 parakeets live in a walk-in enclosure, where visitors feed them with seed sticks.
In 1965 the farm added monkeys, raccoons, loggerhead turtles and a gift shop.
A raccoon's tail has four to six black rings.
Raccoons have nimble, almost hand-like paws that can grasp nuts, fruit and even garbage-can lids.
Raccoons are nocturnal: they search for food at night.
Wild raccoons can live up to 16 years, though about five is typical.
